summary: Report No. 27 of South Korean Interim Government Activities, prepared by the National Economic Board for USAMGIK, covering December 1947 (with November data for transportation, communications, finance and several other sections). It records a month dominated by an acute electric power shortage after North Korea cut supply on 25 November, falling coal, textile and paper output, and food supply concerns despite rice collection reaching 96.2 per cent of quota. Politically it covers the assassination of Chang Duk Soo, the founding of the National Independence Federation, Rhee and Kim Koo's rightist merger, preparation for the UN Commission, and Legislative Assembly disputes with the executive. Tables give prices, trade, finance, refugees (163,253 entered in 1947), and vested property disposal, while the interzone section summarizes North Korean and Soviet radio. Historians will find it useful for the economic statistics and the occupation's own view of politics.
highlights: North Korea cut electric power on 25 November 1947, forcing an Emergency Electric Power Board and executive orders.
Rice collection reached 96.2 per cent of quota by late December 1947.
Retail price index stood at 1,936, about 19 times the August 1945 base.
Chang Duk Soo, Korean Democratic Party head, was assassinated on 3 December by a police sergeant.
National Independence Federation held its first meeting on 20 December.
Agricultural Improvement Service was created on 15 December under Ordinance No. 160.
163,253 refugees from North Korea were counted in 1947; 185,441 in 1946.
Legislative Assembly marked its first anniversary on 12 December 1947.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 27 (December 1947), prepared by the National Economic Board for USAMGIK and filed by the Army Civil Affairs Division, with a map of Korea showing the U.S. and U.S.S.R. zones. The contents list Parts I-VI: population and property custody; production, supply and labor; public services; finance; government and politics; and social affairs including health, education, culture, public information and Korean National Youth.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Explains that the data are mainly for December, but Transportation, Communications, Industrial Production, Mining and Imports and Exports carry November figures. Stresses the difficulty of accurate provincial statistics and the National Economic Board's Statistics Division role. Admits non-economic data are thin, tables repeat two years of figures, and the report is largely American-authored, with Koreans to assume more responsibility.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Population and vested property.

sections.title: Section 1: Population
sections.summary: Concentrates on refugees from North Korea: December's 4,487 was the lowest since February 1947, though about seven times December 1946, and the 1947 total was 163,253 (185,441 in 1946). About 60 per cent went to Seoul or Kyonggi-do, mostly farmers and merchants. Also covers 21,916 illegal Japan entrants, Japanese property shipments, Chinese travel permits and 111 Koreans studying in the U.S.

sections.title: Section 2: Office of Property Custody (Vested Property)
sections.summary: Reports on the Office of Property Custody: a new Corporate Reorganization Sub-section began work, with 285 companies under investigation and 113 preliminary studies done. Loans guaranteed reached 235 million won, mainly through the Chosun Bank. Sales totaled 16 transactions worth 5,205 thousand won, including the first residences. Royal Family estates passed to SKIG control from 1 January 1948; inventories are due by 30 June 1948.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Food, prices, agriculture, mining, industry, allocations, trade and labor.

sections.title: Section 1: Food Supply
sections.summary: Covers the grain year's December flows: 232,213 metric tons of rice collected, 35,038 distributed, and 586,419 on hand. Rice collection reached 96.2 per cent of quota, with Cholla-pukto at 77 per cent; Chungchong-namdo small farmers and a Seoul ration-store fraud are described. Imports totaled 452,473 tons for 1947. The Agriculture memorandum warns that imports of 10,000-34,000 tons monthly are needed to avoid exhausting stocks by July 1948.

sections.title: Section 2: Prices
sections.summary: Seoul's composite retail price index stood at 1,936 in December 1947, over 19 times August 1945, pushed by note issue increases and North Korea's currency conversion. Wholesale index rose to 7,066, driven by coal and power shortages and rice-collection loans, with cotton yarn, raw cotton and silk rising most. Also gives nine-city prices, controlled prices, tobacco increases of 50-233 per cent on 15 December, and civilian supply prices.

sections.title: Section 3: Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries
sections.summary: Sets out the 1948 production goals: 3,211,844 chungbo cropped, 97 per cent of 1940-44, with 1947 rice at 81.6 per cent of goal. Covers livestock goals, seed cotton collection, sericulture cut by power shortages, irrigation, charcoal and fuelwood for Seoul, canned fish, and 220,953 tons of fertilizer shipped. Ordinance 160 created the Agricultural Improvement Service on 15 December, plus 4-H clubs and 325 vested companies.

sections.title: Section 4: Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: November anthracite output fell 5.3 per cent from October while lignite edged up; mines produced about 18 per cent under quota, hit by a late-November power shortage and truck and tire shortages. Only 64,823 tons of bituminous came from Japan in December. The Coal Committee allocated anthracite and emergency coal and studied the pitch shortage. Taichong gold mine was repossessed, copper mines owed 42,208,455 won, and tungsten operations restarted.

sections.title: Section 5: Industrial Production
sections.summary: Reports cover under 10 per cent of 2,012 South Korean factories. November flour output fell 24.3 per cent in the two vested mills, noodles recovered, cotton yarn dropped 13.2 per cent and cloth 15.7 per cent, and paper fell 22.2 per cent. Nails held near the high. Briquettes, coke, cement, brick and rubber goods stayed low for lack of pitch, coal and power. Cigarettes fell 15 per cent.

sections.title: Section 6: Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: Describes how supplies are allocated and distributed in December. Surplus Army clothing is to be dyed and re-marked at the Chosun Boseki plant at Pusanjin; scrap metals and raw materials went to the Bureau of Industry; Kobayashi Mining stockpiles were liquidated. The Federation of Financial Associations distributed 89,820,257 won of goods. An emergency kerosene import of about 2,000,000 gallons was ordered, and Kimchi salt was nearly all distributed.

sections.title: Section 7: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Private imports in November were 463,123,673 won against exports of 107,700,696 won, with 80 to 90 per cent of imports coming via Hong Kong; Pusan handled 48.2 per cent of imports. December government exports to Japan were worth about $134,389. Around 570 tons of scheelite sailed for the United States. Civilian Supply imports in 1947 totaled 988,344 tons, with salt, foodstuffs, fertilizer and bituminous coal detailed.

sections.title: Section 8: Labor
sections.summary: The Department of Labor planned reorganization into four bureaus, pending KILA approval. Power-shortage orders suspended child labor and maximum-hours laws, and part-time vested plants pay a four-hour daily minimum. The Kyongsang Textile dispute over seven discharged union men stalled when the union's ultimatum was rejected by the Mediation Board. 193 unions with 58,556 members were reported. Radio programs ran, and the Industrial Health Association reached 55 doctors.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation, communications, utilities, public works and housing.

sections.title: Section 1: Transportation
sections.summary: Transportation concerns centered on railroads, where lack of bituminous coal forced removal of 58 trains in November. Department receipts fell 21 per cent from October and expenditures 12 per cent. Forty-nine passenger schedules were cancelled, freight tonnage fell 25,000 tons, and under 38 per cent of locomotives were operable. Marine income rose 44 per cent and ships were to carry 45 days of food.

sections.title: Section 2: Communications
sections.summary: Department of Communications receipts rose 18 per cent in November, led by a 7.3 million won rise in telephone income after the 1 October rate increase, while stamp and postal fees fell. Expenditures rose 8 million won and employment 17. Postal deposits dipped slightly and insurance in force rose 3 per cent. Emergency power at Seoul exchanges was inspected, and about 41,000,000 Japanese stamps were ordered destroyed.

sections.title: Section 3: Public Utilities
sections.summary: After North Korea's 25 November notice capping South Korea's draw at 80,000 KW, power delivered fell to 68 million KWH in December (52 million from the north). An Emergency Electric Power Board with legal powers set priorities and bans on heating and cooking. Generating plants ran low; 130-134 Seoul streetcars operated.

sections.title: Section 4: Public Works
sections.summary: December was the low point for Public Works: man-days fell to 72,633 and wage outlay to 14.5 million won. Andong and Namchang bridge projects were inaugurated, over 15 miles of the Seoul-Suwon paving were done, Han River-Ascom City water work finished, and 248 fires cost 244.7 million won.

sections.title: Section 5: Housing
sections.summary: The 40-house low-cost Seoul project was finished and fully occupied, with wood sheathing used against the cold; a site for 1,000 houses is planned. Refugee houses completed under the Welfare Housing Plan reached 5,736 of 15,730 planned, and 200 winterized tents in Seoul were occupied.

sections.title: Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Government and non-government finance.

sections.title: Section 1: Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun note issue reached 33,388 million won, driven by rice-collection loans of 11,772 million and deficit spending. Eight supplemental appropriations of 629 million won raised the budget to 20,089 million. November revenue was 1,225 million won; tax collection lagged, and Civilian Supply deposits stood at 4,463 million won.

sections.title: Section 2: Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: November deposits rose 2,569 million won and loans 16.2 billion, mostly for rice collection and straw and tobacco purchases. Directives tightened loan renewals and watched North Korean currency; a deposit drive added 2.5 billion won. Insurance in force grew, scheelite shipment valued near US$750,000 was sent, and December loans were listed.

sections.title: Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Administration, legislature, politics, legal affairs, police and interzone matters.

sections.title: Section 1: Administration
sections.summary: The month opened with stormy relations between the Legislative Assembly and Deputy Military Governor Helmick over his vetoes, soon smoothed. Civil Service held training courses, 4,108 clerical examinations, and abolished 383 Seoul positions. The National Economic Board approved supplemental budgets, planned cloth distribution to civil servants, and continued staff studies.

sections.title: Section 2: Korean Interim Legislative Assembly
sections.summary: KILA completed passage of the theatrical performances law, settled its dispute with General Helmick over the vetoed bills, and approved governors of Kangwon-do and Chungchong-namdo. Members criticized rice quotas, the Land Reform Bill (3 chungbo ceiling) had its first reading, a no-confidence motion failed 35 to 27, and the first anniversary was held 12 December.

sections.title: Section 3: Political Developments
sections.summary: A quiet month: the moderate National Independence Federation of 15 parties was founded 20 December under Kimm Kiu Sic, and Rhee Syngman and Kim Koo announced a merger in principle that stalled. Parties split over a South-only election and the UN Commission, the Council of 12 Parties lapsed, and Rhee kept attacking General Hodge.

sections.title: Section 4: Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Ordinances 158-160 and Executive Order No. 9 were published. The Opinions Bureau ruled on Labor Mediation Board powers, civil service appointments and the Housing Administration. Prison population stood at 20,718. A rightist terrorism case went to a military commission, the Chang Duk Soo assassination was referred, and judges' resignations were not accepted.

sections.title: Section 5: Police
sections.summary: The section reviews the centralized National Police, set up after 1945 and slowly cut back to police functions. After Chang Duk Soo's assassination on 3 December, police were ordered to stay out of politics and youth groups were restrained. Rice-collection resisters were arrested, and fingerprint requests fell from about 5,000 weekly to 1,760-2,889.

sections.title: Section 6: Interzone Activities
sections.summary: Mail was exchanged at Tosang on 13 and 27 December, with thousands of letters each way. Radio Pyongyang hailed North Korea's currency conversion, a provisional constitution and rejected the UN decision; it announced Ahn Kil's death and coal quotas above 100 per cent. Radio Moscow denounced the UN Commission and MacArthur's Japan policy.

sections.title: Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Health, education, culture, public information, press and youth.

sections.title: Section 1: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: December saw the National Venereal Disease Center open in Seoul on 3 December with 65 beds, 191 patients treated, and a 1,420,000-won rat-control fund for plague prevention. Typhus fell from 117 cases to 4 and typhoid from 239 to 24 against December 1946. Biological output was cut by power shortage; a nutrition survey covered 4,676 families; refugee camps were winterized; the Red Cross lacked trucks.

sections.title: Section 2: Education
sections.summary: The Department of Education completed its 1948-49 budget request of 3,128,979,081 won, nearly 80 percent for common schools, against 1,660,242,480 won the year before. Provincial advisors met 16-17 December on local school taxation. Other items: blind and deaf school enrollment of 370, teacher certification rules from 1 January 1948, Technological Board training projects, the American Language Institute, and research and testing work.

sections.title: Section 3: Culture
sections.summary: The section opens with a survey of Korean literature, poetry and history, then reports on literary societies and the National Library, which logged 291,285 books used and 265,275 readers in 1947. Seven Koreans left to study in the United States and four in Nanking. December also brought Symphony Orchestra concerts, the Korean Broadcasting System's 337 broadcast hours, and the reorganized Royal Asiatic Society.

sections.title: Section 4: Public Information
sections.summary: The Department of Public Information issued 74 press releases in December, including Military Governor Dean's and General Hodge's statements on transferring a terrorism case to an American court and on the murder of Chang Duk Soo. Releases also covered the UN Commission, food, health and education. The Public Opinion Bureau registered 4 parties and 9 publications; a Nonsan field trip found only 35.8 percent thought Americans benefited Korea.

sections.title: Section 5: Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: The Korean press covered the Helmick-KILA dispute over his vetoes of the anti-collaborators bill and temporary constitution, Dean's transfer of the Dai Han Min Chung terror case to a military court, and the failed Rhee-Kim Koo accord. The 2 December murder of Chang Duk Soo overshadowed all, prompting police arrests and press curbs. A women's alliance poll found 106 favoring a North-South leaders' convention, 80 opposed.

sections.title: Section 6: Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Korean National Youth, Inc. grew from 19,270 members in January to 404,585 in December 1947, with committees in the 9 provinces and 108 guns and 15,304 leaders. Leader Lee Bum Suk and Dai Dong's leader issued an 11 December appeal to end mutual slander. Activities included a 11,843,113-seedling planting project, civic work, a Women's Section speakers bureau, and rejection of terrorism charges.
